evidence: But others, by more curious humour led,
That shadows follow them where'er they go.
Thou vainly curious mind which wouldest guess
Above is death--and we are death.

readings.title: Time, flight and memory: short poems of 1821
readings.challenge: Read the six poems through, then pick one image of the sea or a storm and one image of something that lasts after it is gone.
readings.focus: Time as a devouring sea, lovers who defy a storm, and a famous short lyric on what remains when things are gone.
readings.context: Percy Bysshe Shelley (1792–1822) was an English poet and political radical; the text is the Oxford edition of his poems edited by Thomas Hutchinson. In 1821 Shelley was living in Pisa. Emilia Viviani was a young Italian woman whom her father kept in a convent there until a marriage could be arranged; Shelley visited her and wrote poems to her. “Madonna” is Italian for “my lady.” The halcyon is the kingfisher, which in Greek legend calmed the sea while it nested. A barb is a swift Arab horse; a hind is a female deer, and her panting for the brooks echoes Psalm 42. A minster is a great church; “trow” means believe; the lee is the side sheltered from the wind; a portress keeps a gate.

excerpt.locator: Poems Written in 1821: Time, Lines (“Far, far away, O ye”), From the Arabic: An Imitation, To Emilia Viviani, The Fugitives, and To -- (“Music, when soft voices die”), complete as printed; opens “Unfathomable Sea! whose waves are years, Ocean of Time, whose waters of deep woe Are…”; closes “…the beloved's bed; And so thy thoughts, when thou art gone, Love itself shall slumber on.”.

questions.prompt: In “Time,” what is time compared to, and what details make the comparison frightening? How would you answer the closing question?
facilitatorNotes: Time is a shoreless sea whose waves are years and whose salt is “human tears”; it is a beast “sick of prey, yet howling on for more” that throws its wrecks onto the shore of mortality. No one chooses to sail on it, yet everyone does.
The question “Who shall put forth on thee” can mean “who would dare?” or “who could avoid it?” Ask students to choose and defend one.
evidence: Ocean of Time, whose waters of deep woe Are brackish with the salt of human tears!
Who shall put forth on thee, Unfathomable Sea?

questions.prompt: “Lines” addresses birds of memory and birds of the future. Why does the speaker send away the halcyons, and what do the vultures feed on?
facilitatorNotes: The memories bring a “false spring” to a heart in winter, so their calm only hurts. The vultures nest in the future and will feed on “Dying joys”: the past mocks him and the future preys on him.
The two stanzas balance exactly, past against future. Some readers find the despair total; others see a speaker who still has the energy to command the birds away.
evidence: No news of your false spring To my heart's winter bring,
Dying joys, choked by the dead, Will serve your beaks for prey

questions.prompt: “The Fugitives” tells a story in quick, galloping lines. Who is fleeing, from whom, and how does the rhythm fit the story? Compare the lovers’ question at sea with the question that ends “Time.”
facilitatorNotes: Two lovers escape by boat through a storm, while on shore a shamed bridegroom and a “gray tyrant father” curse them. The short rhyming lines and repeated “Come away!” drive forward like the storm and the flight.

The lovers ask “Drive we not free O'er the terrible sea, I and thou?”: they put forth gladly on a sea that “Time” makes terrible. Students can decide whether love answers Time’s question or only forgets it.
evidence: Stands the gray tyrant father,
And 'Drive we not free O'er the terrible sea, I and thou?'

questions.prompt: “Music, when soft voices die” lists things that live on after they end. What are they, and how does the last couplet apply the pattern to the beloved?
facilitatorNotes: Music lives in memory, scent in the sense it quickens and rose leaves are heaped for a bed. So, when the beloved is gone, love will “slumber on” the beloved’s thoughts. The grammar can also mean that love will sleep on, resting on the memory of those thoughts.
Compare it with the gift of flowers in “To Emilia Viviani,” which brings love mixed with sadness. Some readers find “Music” consoling; others hear only loss.
evidence: Music, when soft voices die, Vibrates in the memory--
And so thy thoughts, when thou art gone, Love itself shall slumber on.

readings.title: Delight, change and Napoleon: more poems of 1821
readings.challenge: Two of these poems are about inner feelings and two about power. Read all four, then find one idea that links an inner poem to a political one.
readings.focus: A plea to the Spirit of Delight, a lament for everything that passes, Earth’s scornful answer to a dead conqueror, and a sonnet on ruling oneself.
readings.context: Percy Bysshe Shelley (1792–1822) was an English poet and political radical; the text is the Oxford edition of his poems edited by Thomas Hutchinson. In 1821 Shelley was living in Pisa. Napoleon Bonaparte, the French emperor who conquered much of Europe, died in exile on the island of St Helena in May 1821. This volume has an earlier, different poem also called “Mutability.” A ditty is a simple song and a “merry measure” a lively rhythm; “quick” means living; a knell is the bell tolled for a death, and “knolled” means tolled.

excerpt.locator: Poems Written in 1821: Song (“Rarely, rarely, comest thou”), Mutability (“The flower that smiles to-day”), Lines Written on Hearing the News of the Death of Napoleon, and Sonnet: Political Greatness, complete; opens “Rarely, rarely, comest thou, Spirit of Delight! Wherefore hast thou left me now Many a…”; closes “…throne On vanquished will, quelling the anarchy Of hopes and fears, being himself alone.”.

questions.prompt: In “Song,” why does the Spirit of Delight stay away, and how does the speaker try to win it back? What is clever about the plan in the fourth stanza?
facilitatorNotes: Delight avoids sorrow and comes only to “those who need thee not.” So the speaker sets his sad song “To a merry measure,” hoping to attract delight with pleasure, not pity.
The poem does what it describes: its rhythm is light and quick although its subject is loss. Some readers find the ending hopeful; others notice it is still a request, not an arrival.
evidence: Spirit false! thou hast forgot All but those who need thee not.
Let me set my mournful ditty To a merry measure;
Thou wilt never come for pity, Thou wilt come for pleasure;

questions.prompt: “Mutability” says that we “Survive” our joys. Why is surviving them presented as a misfortune? What is the advice of the last stanza?
facilitatorNotes: Flowers, delight, virtue, friendship and love all pass, but we live on after them, left with nothing we can call ours. The last stanza says to enjoy the bright hours like a dream, knowing we will “wake to weep.”
Compare it with “Song”: both lose delight, but “Song” still pleads for its return, while “Mutability” expects nothing. Students can decide which mood they find more honest.
evidence: But we, though soon they fall, Survive their joy, and all Which ours we call.
Dream thou--and from thy sleep Then wake to weep.

questions.prompt: In the Napoleon poem, the speaker is shocked that Earth goes on. How does Earth answer, and what is her final judgment on Napoleon?
facilitatorNotes: Earth laughs: she takes all her dead into herself, and they feed new life (“I feed on whom I fed”). She calls Napoleon’s life “A torrent of ruin” and tells the living millions to shape their own future, weaving the hopes his glory betrayed into his shame.

Shelley, a republican, had long called Napoleon a tyrant, as in “Feelings of a Republican on the Fall of Bonaparte.” Ask how the poem feels about a great man’s death: grieving, relieved, or indifferent like Earth.
evidence: And canst thou move, Napoleon being dead?
My heart grew warm. I feed on whom I fed.
In terror and blood and gold, A torrent of ruin to death from his birth.

questions.prompt: “Political Greatness” asks, “What are numbers knit By force or custom?” What does the sonnet say true greatness is? How might it answer the career of Napoleon?
facilitatorNotes: Peoples held together by force or habit have no real greatness; poetry and history do not even record their hearts. A man must “rule the empire of himself,” mastering his own will, hopes and fears.
Napoleon ruled empires but not himself, in Shelley’s view. Students can test the sonnet’s claim against a leader they know, and ask whether self-rule is enough to make a nation free.
evidence: What are numbers knit By force or custom?
Man who man would be, Must rule the empire of himself;
being himself alone.

readings.title: An owl, a lament and a letter to a friend: poems of 1821
readings.challenge: Start with the light-hearted first poem, then follow how the next three turn to grief. Mark each line where the speaker talks about himself as already half dead.
readings.focus: A comic moment with an owl, two lyrics of loss and a poem to a close friend that explains why the poet has been avoiding him.
readings.context: Percy Bysshe Shelley (1792–1822) was an English poet and political radical; the text is the Oxford edition of his poems edited by Thomas Hutchinson. In 1821 Shelley was living at Pisa with his wife Mary. Edward Williams and his wife Jane were close friends; Shelley wrote several poems to Jane, and drowned with Edward in a boating accident in 1822. Plucking petals and saying “She loves me—loves me not” is an old fortune-telling game. Pansies were traditionally the flower of thoughts. Words in capitals carry special stress.
readings.contentNote: These poems speak of despair and of death as rest; discuss them with care.

excerpt.locator: Poems Written in 1821: The Aziola, A Lament, Remembrance, and To Edward Williams, complete as printed; opens “'Do you not hear the Aziola cry? Methinks she must be nigh,' Said Mary, as we sate In…”; closes “…are too sad To send to you, but that I know, Happy yourself, you feel another's woe.”.

questions.prompt: In “The Aziola,” what does the speaker think the Aziola is, and why is he so relieved to find out?
facilitatorNotes: He supposes it is “some tedious woman” and is “elate” to learn it is “nothing human, / No mockery of myself to fear or hate”: only a little owl. From then on he loves its sad cry.
The poem is gently funny, and Mary “laughed” at him. But it also shows a man who wants to escape other people. Ask what this prepares for in the poems that follow.
evidence: How elate I felt to know that it was nothing human, No mockery of myself to fear or hate:
'Tis nothing but a little downy owl.

questions.prompt: Compare “A Lament” and “Remembrance.” What has been lost in each, and which images return?
facilitatorNotes: Both mourn a joy that has fled for good: “A Lament” repeats “No more—Oh, never more!”, and “Remembrance” leaves the speaker like “the heart when joy is fled.” Seasons return (“The swallow summer comes again”), but the speaker’s youth and joy do not.
In “Remembrance” he asks for pansies, flowers of thought, to be scattered on “the living grave” he bears. Ask what it means to call oneself a living grave.
evidence: No more--Oh, never more!
Pansies let MY flowers be:
On the living grave I bear

questions.prompt: In “To Edward Williams,” why does the speaker say he now sees his friends “seldomer”?
facilitatorNotes: Their kindness stirs “Griefs that should sleep, and hopes that cannot die”; comfort itself is hard to bear. With them he cannot keep up “the idle mask / Of author” that he wears in the world.
The opening images (the shut-out serpent, the wounded deer, the widowed dove) set him outside a paradise. Ask students what the line “Dear friends, dear FRIEND!” suggests.
evidence: know that I only fly Your looks, because they stir Griefs that should sleep, and hopes that cannot die:
Of acting a forced part in life's dull scene,

questions.prompt: The poem ends by saying “there is a place of peace / Where MY weak heart and all its throbs will cease,” then that the verses are “too sad / To send.” Why send them anyway?
facilitatorNotes: Because the friend, “Happy yourself,” can “feel another’s woe.” The poem is an act of trust: the speaker shares his despair with someone he believes will understand.
Handle this with care. The poems speak of death as rest, but the last lines turn toward a friend. Ask what the poem shows about the value of telling someone how we feel.
evidence: Doubtless there is a place of peace Where MY weak heart and all its throbs will cease.
These verses are too sad To send to you, but that I know, Happy yourself, you feel another's woe.

readings.title: Dirge for the Year
readings.challenge: In each stanza, mark who is told to weep and who to smile. Then decide which voice the poem finally takes.
readings.focus: A funeral song for the old year that keeps hinting the year is only asleep.
readings.context: Percy Bysshe Shelley (1792–1822) was an English poet and political radical; the text is the Oxford edition of his poems edited by Thomas Hutchinson. Shelley dated this poem January 1, 1821; it was published after his death. A dirge is a song of mourning, and its mourners here are the Hours, the children of the Year. A corse is a corpse; a shroud is the cloth wrapped round a body for burial; a sexton digs graves and keeps the churchyard; a bier is the stand on which a coffin is carried. It is read on New Year’s Day, the day the poem is dated.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem: Dirge for the Year (dated January 1, 1821); opens “Orphan Hours, the Year is dead, Come and sigh, come and weep! Merry Hours, smile instead,…”; closes “…doth howl and rave, And April weeps--but, O ye Hours! Follow with May's fairest flowers.”.

questions.prompt: The first stanza calls on two kinds of Hours. What does each say about the Year, and which does the stanza itself seem to believe?
facilitatorNotes: The “Orphan Hours” are told the Year is dead and should weep; the “Merry Hours” are told to smile, because the Year “is but asleep.” The sleeping Year smiles, “Mocking your untimely weeping”: the grief is premature.
Yet the poem is still called a dirge, and the next stanza calls for wailing. Students may say the poem holds both views at once, as the turn of a year does.
evidence: Orphan Hours, the Year is dead,
For the Year is but asleep.
Mocking your untimely weeping.

questions.prompt: Stanzas two and three are each built on a comparison about rocking. What is rocked, and by what? How does the second comparison answer the first?
facilitatorNotes: In the second stanza White Winter rocks the “death-cold Year” as an earthquake rocks a corpse in its coffin, a violent and deathly motion. In the third, “the breath of these rude days” rocks the Year as wind rocks a baby’s cradle hung in a tree, and the Hours are promised that she will rise again.

The same motion is read twice, first as death and then as nursing. Some readers find the coffin image too grotesque for the comfort that follows; others think the shock is the point, since winter looks like death and is not.
evidence: As an earthquake rocks a corse
The tree-swung cradle of a child,
she will arise With new love within her eyes.

questions.prompt: The last stanza turns the months into a funeral procession. Why does it stop at April and May? Does the poem end by mourning the old year or by welcoming the new?
facilitatorNotes: January is the sexton at the grave, February carries the bier, March howls and April weeps; then the Hours are told to follow “with May's fairest flowers.” Funeral flowers become the flowers of spring, so the procession leads out of winter.

A defensible reading: on New Year’s Day the poem treats the year’s death and its rebirth as one event. Others will say the Year never actually rises in the poem, so hope stays a promise and the last scene is still a grave.
evidence: January gray is here, Like a sexton by her grave;
Follow with May's fairest flowers.
